children: Global economic growth has held up surprisingly well against repeated shocks, but that resilience is increasingly coming at the cost of higher interest rates.
In its latest economic outlook, Fitch Ratings raised its global gross domestic product forecast for this year, projecting growth of 2.6%--nearly matching 2025 and close to the long-run trend.
Artificial intelligence has played a leading role, supporting growth in the U.S. and tech powerhouses like South Korea.

Fitch raised U.S. forecasts for both this year and the next by 0.2 percentage points to 2.1%, as consumption holds up despite slowing real household income and the AI capital spending shows no sign of slowing.
"The surge in global IT spending has also helped growth prospects in Mexico and Japan," economists Brian Coulton and Alex Muscatelli wrote in a report.

Fitch raised its growth forecast for India to 6.9% from 6.4%, lifting its outlook for emerging markets--excluding China. It trimmed its 2026 forecast for China to 4.5% as domestic demand indicators weakened again.
The outlook has improved for the four largest eurozone economies too. But Fitch noted that its upward revisions to global growth came alongside substantial increases in interest-rate projections.

"We have seen a big shift in the outlook for real policy interest rates over the next couple of years as a more hawkish chair takes the helm at the Fed, and central banks strive to ensure we do not see the sort of second-round effects from input cost shocks that played out after pandemic," said Coulton, Fitch's chief economist.
The Federal Reserve raised rates for the first time in years last week. Fitch expects another increase in December, followed by a hold at 4.25% next year.
That would put rates at the end of 2027 a full 125 basis points above its June forecast, despite a slight cut its U.S. inflation forecast.

The Bank of Japan has also accelerated tightening, while the European Central Bank has moved rates into mildly restrictive territory to guard against a prolonged rise in energy prices stemming from the Middle East conflict.
Fitch expects the ECB to raise rates once more in October, but sees this year's increases being reversed in 2027 if oil prices normalize.
A sharp fall in oil prices next year seems likely, Fitch said, though it raised its forecast by $5 a barrel to reflect the conflict's longer-than-anticipated duration.
It stressed the uncertainty around that forecast: Geopolitical developments could push oil's average price to $85 a barrel next year, while a rapid recovery in supply could bring it down to $55.
